If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=3x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-3,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=3x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,x,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨y,\,x,\,3x-y⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(3y-x-(3x-y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot \sqrt{11}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{11}}}(4y-4x)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{11}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[4xy-2{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4y-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[2{y}^{2}-2y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$
